title: Sequence and selection
specPoints: 2.2.1 The three basic programming constructs: **sequence**, **selection**, iteration
Selection with `if … elif … else` (Python) / `if … elseif … else … endif` (OCR), including nested selection and `switch/case`
learn: Write programs where the order of lines matters and predict their output
Write `if`, `if/else` and `if/elif/else` statements with correct indentation
Choose between a chain of `elif` and separate `if` statements, and explain the difference
Use nested selection where one decision depends on another
Recognise `switch/case` in OCR pseudocode and convert it to `if/elif`
hook: Two recipes for tea: one says 'boil water, add tea bag, pour'; the other says 'pour, add tea bag, boil water'. Same instructions, different order. Now: 'if the cup is dirty, wash it first'. One line that only sometimes runs. Sequence and selection — you already use both every day.

video.title: If, elif, else: one path through the code
video.brief: 4 minutes. A program as a road: sequence is a straight road, lines lighting up top to bottom. A decision is a fork: the condition is evaluated to True or False and only one branch lights. Then an elif chain as a series of forks where the first true wins and the rest are skipped — animate a mark of 75 passing `>= 90` (false), `>= 70` (true) and skipping the rest. Contrast with three separate ifs where a mark of 95 triggers all three. End with the indentation rule: what is indented belongs to the if.

p: Lines run in order, top to bottom, one at a time. Change the order, change the result. In Try 1 you will swap two lines and watch the output change — the clearest demonstration that the computer does exactly what it is told, in the order it is told.

Selection runs some lines only when a **condition** is true. The condition is any expression that is True or False: `age >= 18`, `name == "Ada"`, `score > best`. Indented lines belong to the `if`; the first unindented line runs regardless.
after: In an `if / elif / else` chain exactly **one** branch runs: the first whose condition is true. Order matters — if the `>= 40` test came first, a mark of 85 would print Pass. OCR pseudocode is the same shape with `then`, `elseif`, `else`, `endif`.

explain.h: Separate ifs are not the same as elif
p: Three separate `if` statements are three independent questions; several can be true. One `if/elif/elif` chain is one question with several answers; exactly one branch runs. Use separate ifs when conditions are unrelated (`if raining: take coat` and `if late: run`); use a chain when the options are mutually exclusive (grades, menu choices).
An `if` inside an `if` asks a second question only when the first was true. Indent one more level. Many nested ifs can often be rewritten with `and` (lesson 5) — both are accepted in the exam.
OCR pseudocode has a `switch` for comparing one value against several fixed options. Python has `match` (3.10+) but you may answer with `if/elif`. You need to **read** switch in exam code:
explain.code:
switch day:
    case "Sat":
        print("Weekend")
    case "Sun":
        print("Weekend")
    default:
        print("Weekday")
endswitch

p: The computer runs the lines from the top down, one at a time. Swap two lines and the result changes.
`if` asks a yes/no question. The indented lines under it run only when the answer is yes. `else` is what to do when the answer is no. `elif` is 'otherwise, try this question'. Only one branch runs.
Two separate `if`s can both happen. An `if / elif` chain picks one. For grades, use a chain.
Ask the second question only if the first answer was yes. Indent it one more time.

keyterms.def: Instructions executed one after another in the order written.
Choosing which instructions to run based on a condition.
An expression that evaluates to True or False.
An if statement inside another if statement.
Spaces at the start of a line showing which block the line belongs to.

try.title: 1. Order matters
p: Run it. Then swap lines 2 and 3 and run again. Explain the difference in one sentence.
try.code:
total = 10
total = total * 2
total = total + 5
print(total)

try.title: 2. Grades
p: Finish the grade program: 90+ is A, 80+ is B, 70+ is C, 60+ is D, below 60 is U. Test with 90, 89, 60, 59 and 100.
try.code:
mark = int(input("Mark out of 100: "))
if mark >= 90:
    grade = "A"
# add the other grades here

print("Grade:", grade)

try.title: 3. Chain or separate?
p: Run with 95. Why do three lines print? Rewrite it so only the best prize prints.

try.title: 4. Nested: cinema tickets
p: Under 12s pay £5; 12–17 pay £7; adults pay £10, but adults who are students pay £7. Finish the program with a nested `if` for the student check.

try.title: 5. PRIMM: predict, run, investigate, modify, make
instructions: Open the selection lesson in the Python IDE and work through the PRIMM steps.
In the Make step, write a program that tells the user which season a month number is in.

check.q: In an `if / elif / else` chain, how many branches run?
opts: None if there is no else
check.fb: First true condition wins; the rest are skipped.

check.q: What tells Python which lines belong to an `if`?
check.fb: Python uses indentation; OCR pseudocode uses endif.

check.q: `if x > 5:` then `if x > 10:` as two separate ifs, with x = 20. What runs?
A grade chain tests `>= 40` before `>= 70`. A mark of 85 prints:
check.fb: Order matters: the first true test wins.

check.q: OCR's `switch … case … default` is most like Python's:
check.fb: One value compared with several fixed options.

exam.q: Write a program that asks the user to enter a temperature and outputs "Cold" if it is below 10, "Warm" if it is between 10 and 24 inclusive, and "Hot" otherwise.
model: Input converted to a number (1). Correct `if temp < 10` branch (1). Correct middle branch — `elif temp <= 24` or `elif temp >= 10 and temp <= 24` (1). `else` branch outputs Hot, and all three outputs present (1).
exam.commentary: The middle condition is the mark that separates students: with an `elif`, `temp <= 24` is enough because `< 10` was already handled. Students who write `if temp < 10 … if temp <= 24 … else` with separate ifs lose a mark because 5 prints Cold *and* Warm.

exam.q: Describe the difference between **sequence** and **selection**, giving an example of each in code.
model: Sequence: instructions executed in order, one after another (1), e.g. `x = 5` then `y = x * 2` (1). Selection: a decision that determines which instructions execute based on a condition (1), e.g. `if x > 3 then print("big") endif` (1).
exam.commentary: Definition + example, twice. Students often give a good definition and a vague example ('an if statement') — write actual code.

exam.q: The following pseudocode contains a logic error. The program should give a 10% discount to customers aged 65 or over and a 20% discount to customers under 18. Identify and correct the error.
exam.code:
age = int(input("Age: "))
if age > 65 then
    discount = 0.1
elseif age < 18 then
    discount = 0.2
else
    discount = 0
endif
model: Line 2 uses `>` so a customer aged exactly 65 gets no discount (1). Correct to `if age >= 65 then` (1).
exam.commentary: Boundary again. Always test the exact number in the question.

home: Write a program for a simple calculator: ask for two numbers and an operator (+, −, ×, ÷) and output the result, with a sensible message for an unknown operator and for dividing by zero. Nested or chained selection — your choice; be ready to justify it.

teacher.timing: 60 min: hook 4 · explain 12 · try 28 · check 5 · exam 8 · homework 3
misconceptions: Separate `if`s used where a chain is needed (Try 3). Let them see three prizes print.
Conditions in a chain in the wrong order (`>= 40` before `>= 70`).
Indentation errors: body not indented, or `else` indented under the `if` body.
Writing `if mark >= 70 and <= 89` (missing the second variable name).
say: 'Only one door opens in an elif chain. Which door, for 85?'
'Indented means inside. Put your finger at the margin and find the first line that isn't indented — that line always runs.'
teacher.skip: Try 5 (PRIMM in the IDE) is a full activity in itself; set it as homework if Try 1–4 take the time.
differentiation: Support: give Try 2 with all the `elif` lines present and only the numbers blank.
Stretch: rewrite Try 4 without nesting using `and`, then explain which version is easier to read and why.
